gate_reasoning: Stage 5 has an unusually strong primary source foundation relative to most supply chain research stages: the TT Club/BSI 2025 Cargo Theft Report (PDF confirmed fetched via markitdown) anchors the most critical SEA-specific claims (Indonesia 5% global, Asia 50% facility, maritime piracy +281%), and four publicly-listed company audited results (Brinks, Loomis, Prosegur, Securitas) provide High-confidence market participant revenue data. The Verisk CargoNet FY2025 and Q2 2025 analyses, ATRI 2025, FBI IC3 PSA, IUMI/TAPA EMEA joint warning, and ESPORG EU study all score High, giving the cargo theft frequency, cost, and law enforcement coordination claims strong primary grounding. The scoring distribution (41% High, 27% Medium, 33% Low) is acceptable for a stage where several categories (market sizing, vendor capabilities, SEA-specific operational data) structurally lack primary sources. The Low-confidence cluster is concentrated in three predictable areas: (1) the three commercial aggregator market sizing figures (correctly pre-flagged Low in the draft), (2) vendor self-reported performance claims for Overhaul, Geotab, G4S, and Brinks SEA operations, and (3) two outdated GPS jammer sources from 2014–2015. The highest-priority weakness for deep research is the recovery-rate benchmark (73%/<20% split, PP5.1-freq-1) — this specific quantification is the central evidentiary claim for the biggest pain point and is currently sourced only from vendor-adjacent trade blogs. The Munich Re 2025 PDF (HTTP 403) and TAPA APAC 2025 data (HTTP 403) should both be attended-fetched to upgrade the Indonesia 14% Asia share from Medium to High. The stage is shippable with these flags: the core structural arguments (SEA cargo security gap, facility-heavy Asia theft pattern, strategic theft growth, coordination failure) are all anchored to High-confidence primary sources; the weak claims are explicitly labeled in the draft and do not undermine the main thesis.
